titleStmt.title: Repetition priming of motor activity mediated by a central pattern generator: the importance of extrinsic vs. intrinsic program initiators

Cropper
Jing

bibl.title: Repetition priming of motor activity mediated by a central pattern generator: the importance of extrinsic vs. intrinsic program initiators

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: In summary, taken together these results and previous work support the idea that repetition priming in the feeding network is mediated by the release of modulatory neurotransmitters from inputs to the CPG.

span.label: repetition priming of motor programs
span.quote: Repetition priming is characterized by increased performance as a behavior is repeated.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: Conventional intracellular and extracellular recording techniques were used.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Priming requires modulatory peptides released by extrinsic CPG inputs; stimulating a core CPG neuron does not release them, so no priming accumulates
span.quote: Rather, it is likely that the appropriate modulators are simply not released when only B63 is stimulated.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: FCAP/CP-2 released from CBI-2 raise the excitability of the ingestive interneuron B40, which is then recruited into later programs and imposes an ingestive B8 firing pattern
span.quote: The recruitment of B40 is likely to result from a peptide (i.e., FCAP/CP-2)-mediated excitability increase.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Priming is stored as persistent modulator-induced changes in the pattern-generating interneurons B20 and B40 inside the feeding network rather than presynaptically in the input terminals
span.quote: However, taken together our data strongly suggest that effects of repetition priming are at least partially mediated by effects of modulators on pattern generating interneurons within the feeding network (i.e., B20 and B40).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Carry-over between behaviours occurs only when the interneuron modified by the first behaviour is also part of the circuit recruited by the second, which is why switch costs are asymmetric
span.quote: This will happen if neurons that are modified during the first type of activity are part of the circuitry activated during the second type.

span.label: Somatic recordings used to rule out indirect recruitment of the CPG inputs may not reflect activity at those inputs' terminals.
span.quote: However, somatic recordings do not necessarily reflect electrical activity in the terminals of CPG inputs (see, e.g., Nusbaum 1994 ).

span.label: An additional contribution from modulation of the motor neuron B8 itself is not excluded.
span.quote: Thus our findings do not rule out an effect of input activation on the properties of B8 itself.

span.label: six to ten control measurements taken first, then B40 current injections interleaved with the CBI-2 stimulation trains
span.note: eliminates: drift in the preparation over the course of a long intracellular recording - the baseline is established first and the two conditions then alternate rather than running in sequence
span.quote: After 6–10 control measurements, B40 current injections were interleaved with three 30-s trains of CBI-2 stimulation (15 ms, 10 Hz; current adjusted to yield 1 spike/pulse).

span.label: repetition priming
span.quote: repetition priming is characterized by increased performance as a behavior is repeated. Although repetition priming is observed in many species and contexts (see, e.g., Epuru et al. 1995 ; Schacter and Buckner 1998 ; Sharma et al. 2003 ; Sinnamon et al. 2000 ), there have been relatively few studies that have characterized underlying mechanisms

span.label: central pattern generator
span.quote: It consists of a central pattern generator (CPG) (e.g., Hurwitz et al. 1997 ; Hurwitz and Susswein 1996 ; Jing et al. 2004 ; Susswein and Byrne 1988 ) and inputs to the CPG

span.label: B63
span.quote: B63 is a buccal interneuron that is part of the CPG that generates both ingestive and egestive motor programs in Aplysia

span.label: CBI-2
span.quote: The ingestive input to the CPG (neuron CBI-2) releases the peptides feeding circuit activating peptide and cerebral peptide 2, which produce an ingestive pattern of activity

span.label: B40
span.quote: we demonstrate that either CBI-2 stimulation or exogenous application of these peptides increases the excitability of B40

span.label: B20
span.quote: After stimulation of the egestive input (the EN), we demonstrate recruitment of a different interneuron (B20) during subsequent B63 triggered motor programs

span.label: chemical coding
span.quote: Previous data suggest a chemical coding model: ingestive and egestive inputs to the feeding central pattern generator (CPG) release different modulators, which act via different second messengers to prime motor activity in different ways

span.label: task switching
span.quote: Potentially this arrangement could have interesting consequences for task switching, i.e., the cessation of one type of motor activity and the initiation of a second type

span.label: negative biasing
span.quote: Negative biasing is observed when motor programs are triggered by stimulating CBI-2 after EN-induced repetition priming. The first cycle of induced activity is egestive

span.label: repetition priming as defined here - increased performance as a behaviour is repeated, measured in a dissected Aplysia ganglion, with no reference to memory, awareness or a subject → media priming as defined in Hoewe2020 (in this corpus), which REQUIRES that the person be unable to mentally trace the source of the influence, and is restricted to System 1
span.note: THE SAME WORD AT BOTH ENDS OF ITS POSSIBLE EXTENSION, IN ONE CORPUS. One paper applies `priming` to a preparation with no subject at all - a buccal ganglion on a dish, where the criterion is that a motor pattern becomes better articulated on repetition. Another makes the ABSENCE OF A SUBJECT'S AWARENESS the defining criterion, and proposes an operational test built entirely on asking the person what they noticed. **A definition requiring unawareness and a definition with nobody to be unaware cannot be the same definition**, yet neither paper marks the word as belonging to another field. Both are ordinary uses in their own literatures. This is not a disagreement and not an error by either: it is the extension of a term stretched past the point where one definition can cover it, which is the object this project was assembled to document. The schema has no relation type for `these records use one term at incompatible scopes`; `renamed-across-fields` is the closest and it is wrong, because the name did not change - only what it can be true of. See Q-731, and Q-632 for the missing types.
span.quote: repetition priming is characterized by increased performance as a behavior is repeated. Although repetition priming is observed in many species and contexts (see, e.g., Epuru et al. 1995 ; Schacter and Buckner 1998 ; Sharma et al. 2003 ; Sinnamon et al. 2000 ), there have been relatively few studies that have characterized underlying mechanisms

span.label: repetition priming, in an invertebrate preparation - INCREASED PERFORMANCE AS A BEHAVIOUR IS REPEATED, and nothing else. No memory, no awareness, no subject. Set beside Hoewe2020, where the same word requires that a person be unable to trace an influence, this is the widest extension of the term in the corpus
span.quote: repetition priming is characterized by increased performance as a behavior is repeated. Although repetition priming is observed in many species and contexts (see, e.g., Epuru et al. 1995 ; Schacter and Buckner 1998 ; Sharma et al. 2003 ; Sinnamon et al. 2000 ), there have been relatively few studies that have characterized underlying mechanisms

span.label: how priming MANIFESTS here - not faster or stronger but better ARTICULATED: the first cycle of a program is neither ingestive nor egestive, and repetition makes it become one. The measured quantity is the definiteness of a pattern, not the size of a response
span.quote: if an input is stimulated in a quiescent preparation, the first cycle of the motor program is poorly defined (i.e., it is neither ingestive nor egestive). However, as input activation is repeated, phase relationships change such that program articulation develops, e.g., if an ingestive input is repeatedly stimulated motor activity becomes clearly ingestive

span.label: `prime` in the authors' own scare quotes - used for the derived case, where a program triggered from inside the CPG shows priming only because extrinsic inputs were stimulated first. They mark the word when the thing does not meet their own paradigm case
span.quote: This suggests that it should be possible to “prime” motor programs triggered from within the CPG by first stimulating extrinsic modulatory inputs

span.label: the negative result read carefully - the authors decline the strong reading of their own null: nothing PRECLUDES priming of B63-induced programs, the modulators are simply not released when only B63 is stimulated. An absence of an effect is read as an absence of a cause, not as an impossibility
span.quote: Our data therefore indicate that nothing “precludes” the priming of B63-induced motor programs. Rather, it is likely that the appropriate modulators are simply not released when only B63 is stimulated

span.label: builds-on → the chemical coding model of repetition priming developed from the radula opener circuitry (Friedman et al. 2015; Friedman and Weiss 2010)
span.quote: Our results are therefore consistent with the chemical coding model developed as a result of previous experiments conducted on the radula opener circuitry ( Friedman et al. 2015 ; Friedman and Weiss 2010 ).

span.label: replicates → previous demonstrations that unprimed CBI-2- and EN-induced buccal motor programs have intermediate rather than ingestive or egestive characteristics (Dacks et al. 2012; Friedman et al. 2009; Proekt et al. 2004)
span.quote: We confirmed these results, demonstrating that 80% of the unprimed BMPs induced by CBI-2 were classified as intermediate, as were 75% of the unprimed BMPs induced by EN stimulation ( Fig. 2 ).

span.label: B63 —causes→ repetition priming
span.note: direction on the measure: no-change · strength of the relation: 0.1 — the record marks this weak — THE LOAD-BEARING NEGATIVE. Repetition alone does not prime; the priming belongs to the extrinsic inputs. The paper predicted this before testing it - `if priming is in fact the result of input activation, then we would expect the answer to be no` - which is what makes the null a result rather than a gap.
span.quote: When motor programs are repeatedly generated by stimulating B63 with a short ISI, repetition priming does not occur

span.label: CBI-2 —causes→ repetition priming
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.9 — And the KIND of priming follows the input, not the repetition - which is the chemical coding model's whole content.
span.quote: The ingestive input, the neuron CBI-2, contains two peptides: cerebral peptide 2 (CP-2) and feeding circuit activating peptide (FCAP) ( Koh et al. 2003 ; Koh and Weiss 2005 ; Morgan et al. 2000 ; Sweedler et al. 2002 ), which play an important role in the induction of repetition priming

span.label: CBI-2 —causes→ B40
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.9 — THE LOCALISATION, and the reason it is convincing: the same effect is produced by stimulating the input OR by applying its peptides directly, so the route is chemical rather than synaptic.
span.quote: we demonstrate that either CBI-2 stimulation or exogenous application of these peptides increases the excitability of B40

span.label: repetition priming —causes→ negative biasing
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — The consequence for task switching, and it follows from persistence: B20 is left more excitable by egestive priming and is active during ingestive programs too, so the modification carries into the next behaviour.
span.quote: Negative biasing is observed when motor programs are triggered by stimulating CBI-2 after EN-induced repetition priming. The first cycle of induced activity is egestive

span.label: chemical coding —causes→ repetition priming
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — Stated as what the data SUGGEST rather than as established here - the supporting work is cited to Friedman et al. - and weighted for that. The content is that WHICH modulator is released decides which kind of priming occurs, so the identity of the input is the identity of the effect.
span.quote: Thus data suggest that chemical coding plays a role in the context of repetition priming in that different inputs to the feeding CPG release different modulators, which act via different second messengers to configure motor activity in different ways

span.label: B20 —causes→ negative biasing
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.75 — Hedged by the authors - `likely to be at least partially responsible` - and weighted for it. The mechanism is specific even where the claim is cautious: B20 receives input during BOTH program types, so a modification made during egestive priming is still in place when an ingestive program is triggered.
span.quote: Thus the modifications of B20 that occur during egestive repetition priming are likely to be at least partially responsible for the negative biasing that has been described in the feeding circuitry

span.label: paired t-test
span.quote: Two-group comparisons were made with paired t -tests.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: Data with more than two groups were analyzed with an appropriate ANOVA.

span.label: repeated-measures ANOVA
span.quote: Significant effects of CBI-2 stimulation were observed [ Fig. 4 , B–D ; 1-way repeated-measures ANOVA: F (2,18) = 41.88, P < 0.0001].

span.label: Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons
span.quote: When significance was detected ( P < 0.05), pairwise comparisons were performed with t -tests with Bonferroni corrections for significance.

span.label: correlation
span.quote: Pooled analysis of all time points within and across preparations revealed a significant correlation between B40 firing and B8 retraction activity ( r = 0.7665, P < 0.0001, n = 103 BMPs).

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: Digitized electrophysiological recordings were plotted with CorelDRAW v. 13 (Ottawa, ON, Canada), and data are expressed as means ± SE.

span.label: Repeatedly triggering feeding motor programs from inside the central pattern generator, by stimulating interneuron B63, produced no repetition priming: B8 firing stayed low in both protraction and retraction across repetitions.
span.quote: When B63 was stimulated we found no significant improvement in response articulation ( Fig. 3 ).

span.label: Repetition priming did occur when the same programs were driven through extrinsic inputs, the esophageal nerve or CBI-2, showing priming depends on which element triggers the program rather than on CPG activation per se.
span.quote: In contrast, repetition priming was observed when motor programs were induced by stimulating either the EN or CBI-2 ( Fig. 3 B ).

span.label: Unprimed programs were mostly intermediate (neither ingestive nor egestive) whichever element triggered them: 80% for CBI-2, 75% for the esophageal nerve, and 94% for B63.
span.quote: We confirmed these results, demonstrating that 80% of the unprimed BMPs induced by CBI-2 were classified as intermediate, as were 75% of the unprimed BMPs induced by EN stimulation ( Fig. 2 ).

span.label: Priming the ingestive input CBI-2 first, then switching to B63 to trigger programs, made the B63-triggered programs ingestive with a fivefold rise in retraction-phase B8 firing that later returned to baseline, showing the priming is stored postsynaptically in the core network.
span.quote: These data suggest that CBI-2-induced repetition priming modifies properties of the core network postsynaptic to CBI-2.

span.label: Priming the egestive esophageal-nerve input first likewise made subsequent B63-triggered programs egestive, with a threefold rise in protraction-phase B8 firing that recovered within 15 minutes.
span.quote: These data suggest that repeated stimulation of the EN also induces repetition priming by modifying properties of the core feeding network.

span.label: Bath application of the CBI-2 peptides FCAP and CP-2 reproduced the ingestive signature, raising retraction-phase B8 firing to over 250% of baseline without significantly changing protraction firing.
span.quote: FCAP/CP-2 superfusion partially mimicked effects of CBI-2 stimulation, i.e., it had a significant effect on the retraction-phase firing frequency of B8 [1-way repeated-measures ANOVA: F (2,10) = 39.93, P < 0.0001], increasing it to >250% of baseline ( Fig. 6 , A and C ).

span.label: Bath application of the esophageal-nerve peptide SCPb reproduced the egestive signature, raising protraction-phase B8 firing to over 250% of baseline.
span.quote: In contrast, SCP b superfusion had a significant effect on the protraction-phase firing frequency of B8 [ Fig. 6 , B and D ; 1-way repeated-measures ANOVA: F (2,6) = 33.95, P = 0.0005], namely, it increased the frequency to >250% of baseline

span.label: Ingestive priming acted by making the ingestive pattern-generating interneuron B40 more excitable, so that it was recruited into subsequent B63-triggered programs with more spikes per current pulse, shorter spike latency and a depolarized resting potential.
span.quote: These data indicate that ingestive priming increases the excitability of the interneuron B40 and increases its firing frequency during B63-induced motor programs.

span.label: Egestive priming instead recruited the egestive interneuron B20, whose protraction firing frequency more than doubled after esophageal-nerve stimulation.
span.quote: EN stimulation had a significant effect on firing frequency [ Fig. 9 , A and B 1 ; 1-way repeated-measures ANOVA: F (2,8) = 16.99, P = 0.0013]. It more than doubled, increasing to 5.1 ± 0.5 Hz [post hoc comparison; t (4) = 5.48, P = 0.0018].

span.label: Because B20 receives excitatory drive during both ingestive and egestive programs whereas B40 receives it only during ingestive ones, the authors explain the observed asymmetry of task switching: negative biasing when switching from egestive to ingestive but positive biasing in the opposite direction.
span.quote: We suggest that this at least partially accounts for the asymmetries in task switching that have been observed in the feeding network, i.e., negative biasing in the egestive-ingestive direction and positive biasing in the ingestive-egestive direction.

span.label: repetition priming
span.quote: Repetition priming is characterized by increased performance as a behavior is repeated.

span.label: ingestion (ingestive program)
span.quote: During ingestion the radula is open during protraction and closed during retraction, which pulls food in ( Morton and Chiel 1993a , 1993b ).

span.label: egestion (egestive program)
span.quote: During egestion, the radula is closed during protraction and open during retraction ( Morton and Chiel 1993a , 1993b ); this pushes food out.

span.label: ingestive motor program (operational classification criteria)
span.quote: More specifically, motor programs were classified as ingestive if they met the following three criteria: the protraction-phase B8 firing frequency was <3.5 Hz, the retraction-phase B8 firing frequency was >4.5 Hz, and the ratio obtained by dividing the B8 firing frequency during protraction by the B8 firing frequency during retraction was <0.65.

span.label: protraction phase (in vitro definition)
span.quote: In vitro, protraction is defined as the phase of the motor program in which there is activity in the I2 nerve (since it contains axons of radula protraction motor neurons)

span.label: chemical coding model of repetition priming
span.term: chemical coding model of repetition priming
span.quote: This model postulates that repetition priming is induced by modulators released from CPG inputs, with the nature of priming depending on the input activated and the type of modulator released.

span.label: negative biasing
span.quote: Negative biasing is observed when motor programs are triggered by stimulating CBI-2 after EN-induced repetition priming.

span.label: task switching
span.quote: Potentially this arrangement could have interesting consequences for task switching, i.e., the cessation of one type of motor activity and the initiation of a second type.

span.label: element stimulated to trigger the motor program (B63 vs CBI-2 vs esophageal nerve)
span.term: element stimulated to trigger the motor program (B63 vs CBI-2 vs esophageal nerve)
span.quote: Preparations were rested for >15 min, and a single cycle of a BMP was induced by stimulating B63, an ingestive input to the CPG (CBI-2), or an egestive input to the CPG (the EN) ( Fig. 1 C ).

span.label: exogenous peptide application (FCAP/CP-2 or SCPb superfusion)
span.term: exogenous peptide application (FCAP/CP-2 or SCPb superfusion)
span.quote: After four programs in control saline, we superfused a peptide solution for a total of 15 min at 10 −6 M and then returned to the control saline for 20 min.

span.label: B8 firing frequency during protraction vs retraction
span.term: B8 firing frequency during protraction vs retraction
span.quote: Motor programs were classified as ingestive, egestive, or intermediate by determining the relative B8 firing frequency during protraction vs. retraction ( Fig. 1 B ).

span.label: B40 excitability (spikes evoked per constant-current pulse)
span.term: B40 excitability (spikes evoked per constant-current pulse)
span.quote: Before CBI-2 was stimulated, 8.7 ± 0.9 spikes were triggered by current injection into B40. After the last burst of CBI-2 activity, 19.2 ± 2.3 spikes were triggered [post hoc comparison; t (4) = 7.26, P = 0.0003].

span.label: latency to spike initiation in B40
span.term: latency to spike initiation in B40
span.quote: CBI-2 stimulation also resulted in a significant decrease in latency (i.e., as measured by the difference between the beginning of the injected current pulse and the first B40 spike)

span.label: interstimulus interval between successive program cycles (fixed at 30 s)
span.term: interstimulus interval between successive program cycles (fixed at 30 s)
span.quote: We used a protocol in which we triggered successive cycles of a motor program with an interstimulus interval (ISI) of 30 s (i.e., there was 30 s between each cycle of the motor program).

span.label: injected current into B40 (set to a fixed ~10 spikes/pulse baseline)
span.term: injected current into B40 (set to a fixed ~10 spikes/pulse baseline)
span.quote: Injected current was adjusted to yield a baseline of ∼10 spikes/pulse.

span.label: high-divalent cation saline used to block polysynaptic pathways
span.term: high-divalent cation saline used to block polysynaptic pathways
span.quote: To suppress polysynaptic connections, preparations were bathed in a high-divalent cation solution (HiDi).

span.label: superfusion rate held at 0.3 ml/min in all experiments
span.term: superfusion rate held at 0.3 ml/min in all experiments
span.quote: In all experiments, including those involving peptides, preparations were superfused at a rate of 0.3 ml/min.

span.label: 94% — Share of unprimed buccal motor programs triggered from inside the CPG (B63) that were classified as intermediate
span.quote: Similar results were obtained with B63 stimulation ( Fig. 2 ), namely, 94% of the induced BMPs were intermediate.

span.label: 1.2 ± 0.4 Hz to 6.1 ± 0.8 Hz — Fivefold increase in B8 retraction-phase firing in B63-triggered programs caused by prior CBI-2 (ingestive) priming
span.quote: A post hoc comparison indicated that there was a fivefold increase in the B8 firing frequency during retraction, i.e., the firing frequency before CBI-2 stimulation was 1.2 ± 0.4 Hz and the frequency after CBI-2 stimulation was 6.1 ± 0.8 Hz [ t (9) = 7.8, P < 0.0001].

span.label: 1.0 ± 0.2 Hz to 3.1 ± 0.5 Hz — Threefold increase in B8 protraction-phase firing in B63-triggered programs caused by prior esophageal-nerve (egestive) priming, recovering within 15 min
span.quote: A post hoc comparison indicated a threefold increase in firing frequency. It went from 1.0 ± 0.2 Hz to 3.1 ± 0.5 Hz [ t (7) = 6.35, P < 0.0001] and recovered within 15 min, falling to 1.1 ± 0.3 Hz [ t (7) = 0.34, P = 1].

span.label: 9.8 ± 5.7% to 87.5 ± 4.2% — Fraction of the protraction phase during which B40 was active, before versus after CBI-2-induced priming
span.quote: Thus it increased from 9.8 ± 5.7% to 87.5 ± 4.2% [post hoc comparison; t (4) = 10.65, P < 0.001].

span.label: 8.7 ± 0.9 to 19.2 ± 2.3 spikes — Spikes evoked in B40 by a fixed 3-s current pulse before and after three trains of CBI-2 stimulation, i.e. the excitability increase
span.quote: Before CBI-2 was stimulated, 8.7 ± 0.9 spikes were triggered by current injection into B40. After the last burst of CBI-2 activity, 19.2 ± 2.3 spikes were triggered [post hoc comparison; t (4) = 7.26, P = 0.0003].

span.label: r = 0.7665, P < 0.0001, n = 103 BMPs — Correlation between B40 firing and B8 retraction-phase activity pooled across time points and preparations
span.quote: Pooled analysis of all time points within and across preparations revealed a significant correlation between B40 firing and B8 retraction activity ( r = 0.7665, P < 0.0001, n = 103 BMPs).

span.label: r = 0.8296, P < 0.0001, n = 56 BMPs — Correlation between B20 firing and B8 firing during protraction
span.quote: Analysis of all 56 programs recorded revealed a significant correlation between B20 and B8 firing during protraction ( r = 0.8296, P < 0.0001, n = 56 BMPs).

span.label: 1.0 ± 0.2 Hz vs 1.4 ± 0.2 Hz, P = 0.18 — B8 protraction and retraction firing in unprimed B63-triggered programs, statistically indistinguishable between phases
span.quote: In B63-induced BMPs, B8 fired at a mean rate of 1.0 ± 0.2 Hz during protraction and 1.4 ± 0.2 Hz during retraction, with no significant difference between the two phases of the motor program [paired t -test; t (17) = 1.38, P = 0.18].
